title: 6 Best Zapier Alternatives for AI Agents in 2026 (and How Each Handles Exceptions)
summary: Zapier Agents handle the happy path across 9,000+ apps. Approvals, activity caps and failed runs are where teams look around. Six alternatives compared on what each one does when a run goes wrong, all checked November 24, 2026.
body_markdown:
*For teams that need AI agents instead of trigger-action automations, the strongest Zapier alternatives are Make, n8n, Gumloop, Lindy, Relevance AI and Activepieces. Zapier Agents handle the happy path across 9,000+ apps, and Zapier's own help docs show where the friction starts: approvals are prompt instructions, every action burns an activity, and a run that breaks just stops. This guide compares the six on what each one does when a run goes wrong, with facts checked November 24, 2026.*


## What is the best Zapier alternative for AI agents?


It depends on where your team already works and who fixes things when they break. The short version:


- Best for teams already on Make: Make, whose agents live inside scenarios backed by a mature error-handling system.
- Best for engineering control: n8n, which pauses a run for human review per tool and runs self-hosted.
- Best for AI-native visual building: Gumloop, with connector-level approval modes.
- Best for a Slack-first AI teammate: Lindy, whose guardrails sit in shared Slack threads.
- Best for governed agent fleets: Relevance AI, with per-connection approval modes and escalation alarms.
- Best for self-hosted approval gates: Activepieces, where a paused run holds its place for 30 days and the approver needs no seat.

## Why teams replace Zapier Agents in 2026


The reasons come from Zapier's own documentation, not from competitor marketing.


Approvals are instructions, not controls. Zapier's help doc on agent approvals tells you to add a sentence like "ask for my confirmation through \[messaging app\]" to the agent's instructions, give the agent a messaging action, and return to the agent screen to approve. Inside Zaps, a Human in the Loop step sits after the Agents step. It works, but it is a prompt convention plus plumbing, not a per-tool gate with an audit trail.


The bill counts actions, not outcomes. Zapier's activity doc lists the ways a run burns quota: each action is an activity, processing ten new leads multiplies the count by ten, every knowledge-source lookup and every web search counts, and a run has a built-in cap of 10 activities on Free plans and 40 on paid. For an agent that follows up across apps all day, the meter runs on every step.


The platform is mid-migration. Both help pages we checked carry the same note: Zapier is moving Agents to "AI by Zapier". Teams rebuilding agents on a moving target are re-evaluating the platform anyway.


And the deeper one: an agent that owns a goal, like keeping the pipeline clean or answering every support email within a day, needs exception handling and follow-up as first-class features. A trigger-action engine treats both as workarounds.


## 1. Make


Make is the shortest move for teams already building scenarios there.


Its AI agents live inside scenarios: a trigger starts the flow, the agent gets instructions, tools and knowledge, and the surrounding modules keep running. That placement is the appeal. Your agent sits in the middle of flows you already operate, with the same connections and the same history.


The error side is where Make is strongest of the six. A failed module stops the run and, with incomplete executions on, it lands in a manual queue Make calls the Incomplete executions tab. If the same failure keeps happening, you add an error handler, a module that intercepts the failure and applies predefined logic: Resume substitutes a value and continues, Retry waits and tries again, Break moves the run aside for later. Make also auto-disables a scenario's schedule after repeated consecutive failures, so a broken flow stops burning operations while you investigate.


What it does not give you: a goal. The agent works when a scenario runs, nobody owns the outcome between runs, and the follow-up loop, chasing the missing phone number and coming back tomorrow, is yours to build.


Choose Make if your automations already live there and you want judgment inside them. Adding agents to an empty Make account just to have agents is more setup than it sounds.


## 2. n8n


n8n is the pick for engineering teams that want to keep the infrastructure.


Its agents are first-class artifacts next to workflows, with their own instructions, tools and knowledge base, and n8n ships a real per-tool approval gate: when a tool that needs review is about to run, the workflow pauses and sends the request, tool name and parameters to a reviewer in Slack, Telegram, n8n Chat or another channel. The reviewer approves and the tool runs with the AI-specified input, or denies and the action is canceled. You choose which tools need review, which is the right shape for irreversible actions like deleting data or sending external messages.


Two things to weigh. Agents are in Preview, and n8n says so on the docs page: behavior may change while the feature develops. And you run the instance, self-hosted from version 2.32.3 up or on n8n Cloud, so patching and uptime are your team's job.


Choose n8n if your engineers want error paths and approval gates as workflow logic they control, and you accept preview-grade agent features in exchange.


## 3. Gumloop


Gumloop is the AI-native visual builder closest to what Zapier Agents tries to be, with approval controls designed in rather than bolted on.


Every connector you add gets an approval setting: Always allow, Ask each time, Ask for writes/deletes, Never allow or Custom per tool. Gumloop sorts each connector's tools into read-only and write groups, so Ask for writes/deletes gives you a sensible default in one click: the agent reads freely and pauses before anything that changes data. When a gated tool call comes up, the agent pauses with an approval card naming the tool and the proposed action, and the request arrives in-app, as a Slack DM or in the chat thread.


That is the same pause-and-approve shape the others have. What Gumloop does not add is an owner for the run between approvals: the run resumes or adjusts when you answer, and the broader goal lives in your head, not in the product.


Choose Gumloop if you want Zapier-style visual building with AI agents at the center and approval defaults that need no prompt hack.


## 4. Lindy


Lindy takes the AI-employee framing literally: one assistant that takes on work across your tools, with routines for anything that repeats.


Its guardrails live where your team already works. In shared Slack threads, each integration gets one of three settings: Always allow, Require approval, or Don't offer, which hides write actions for that tool entirely. When approval is needed, Lindy posts Approve and Deny buttons in the thread. That is a lower-friction loop than a dashboard: the reviewer decides where the conversation already is.


Lindy also published its answer to the scarier failure mode. Its engineering post describes a validator: a second LLM call reviews every side-effectual action before it runs, checking the agent's justification against what the user asked for. They built it after approving every action by hand made the product unusable, and trusting the agent alone got their CEO a dozen calendar invites he never requested. It is the most detailed public writeup on agent guardrails of the six.


Choose Lindy for recurring personal or team work in Slack and email. The credit-based pricing and the single-assistant shape make it less of a fit for fleet-style automation.


## 5. Relevance AI


Relevance AI is built for teams running many agents at once, and its approval system reflects that scale.


Every connection between an agent and a tool, or between two agents, gets a behavior setting: Auto run, Approval required or Let agent decide, where the agent asks for approval only when its context or confidence is thin. Approval requests surface in the Workforce task view, and since the November 2, 2026 changelog, Workforce approval steps carry Approve and Reject buttons directly in Slack. The October 20, 2026 changelog added task alarms: an alarm fires when the share of failed, approval-blocked or escalated tasks crosses a threshold you set, and alerts go to email, Slack or Teams.


That last piece matters more than it sounds. On a fleet of agents, the question is not whether one run failed but whether the failure rate is drifting up this week, and Relevance is the only one of the six with a built-in answer.


Choose Relevance AI for governed multi-agent operations. For a single agent doing one job, the workforce scaffolding is more than you need.


## 6. Activepieces


Activepieces is the open-source option: self-host it, keep your data in your infrastructure, and put a person in front of any step that matters.


Its agent builder pairs agents with human approvals as a first-class step: a paused run keeps its place for 30 days, and the person approving needs no account and no seat, which matters when the approver is a finance person who will never log into your automation tool. Runs resume from checkpoints, with every tool call written to the run log.


One limitation to plan around, stated plainly on their product page: the agent remembers nothing between runs. Knowledge comes from files you upload or tables you keep current, with no live sync from SharePoint, Drive or Notion. For recurring work that should always consult maintained reference data, a stateless agent is a feature, not a bug. For follow-up chains that depend on what happened last time, it is not.


Choose Activepieces when self-hosting and seat-free approvals outweigh the missing memory.


## Tools we looked at and left off the list


- AutoGPT: the open-source agents platform fits power users who want to self-host and tinker, but the approval and exception story is thinner than the six above and the setup cost is real.
- Relay.app: the workflow tool known for native human-approval steps shut down in September 2026 and deleted all accounts and run history. If you are migrating off Relay, the approval-step pattern you liked lives in n8n, Gumloop and Relevance AI.


## How to choose


The decision is about failure behavior, not feature lists.


If your automations already exist somewhere, start there. Make agents live in your scenarios, and its error handlers are the most mature of the six. If you are starting fresh, decide who reviews the agent's work. Engineers with opinions about error paths: n8n. Operations people living in Slack: Lindy for one assistant, Relevance AI for a fleet. Teams that want to own the stack: Gumloop's approval defaults on a hosted build, Activepieces on your own servers.


Then pressure-test one scenario before you commit. Pick the run you are most afraid of getting wrong, and check what the platform does when it fails mid-run, who gets asked, and whether anyone follows up tomorrow. Every tool here answers that question in its docs. Where the docs go quiet, keep looking.

## FAQ


### Is Zapier good for building AI agents?


For trigger-action automation, yes, and its 9,000+ app catalog is hard to beat. For agents that own recurring goals, its approval model is prompt-based instructions and the per-run activity caps, 10 on Free and 40 on paid plans, meter every step. It is a reasonable start and a common ceiling.


### What is the cheapest Zapier alternative for AI agents?


n8n and Activepieces are open source and free to self-host; you pay in ops time instead of a subscription. Cloud pricing changes often across this category, so check current pricing pages before you compare.


### Can AI agents ask a human before taking an action?


Yes, on all six tools above, and on Zapier itself through instruction-based approvals. The difference is granularity: n8n gates per tool, Gumloop per connector with write/delete defaults, Relevance AI per connection, Activepieces with 30-day holds, Lindy in Slack threads.


### What happened to Relay.app?


Relay.app shut down in September 2026 and deleted accounts, workflows and run history. Its human-approval workflow pattern survives in the tools listed above.
